docs.title: rulewise documentation
docs.text:
rulewise mines association rules and keeps only those that survive exact statistical testing, multiple-testing correction and a simplification (productivity) test. It also reports honest intervals and a validation report.

Start with the five-minute example below, then use these pages:

page what it covers API reference parameters, attributes, methods, output columns and input formats Methodology exact tests, productivity, corrections, holdout and direct modes Limitations assumptions, power, redundancy, basket-size effects and other failure modes Comparison measured evidence against mlxtend and the classical workflow Groceries tutorial real supermarket baskets end to end Classification tutorial rule-based classification on Mushrooms and Titanic Publishing release checklist, build and upload

docs.title: Five-minute example
docs.text:
from rulewise import RuleMiner

baskets = (
    [["a", "b", "c"]] * 150
    + [["a", "b"]] * 50
    + [["c"]] * 50
    + [["d", "e"]] * 50
)

miner = RuleMiner(min_support=0.2, n_bootstrap=0).fit(baskets)
print(miner.summary())

This toy example finds six rules, including the symmetric a -> b and b -> a and the partially productive a -> c and c -> a. On real data use a support floor that leaves enough candidates, for example 0.005 to 0.01 for supermarket baskets.

docs.title: The one idea
docs.text:
A classical miner answers: which rules are frequent and confident? rulewise answers: which rules are frequent, confident, and still useful after accounting for every rule we tried?

That difference is measured, not asserted. On 500 pure-noise datasets, mlxtend returned rules in 500 of them (mean 1,929 rules); rulewise returned a rule in 4 (0.8%). On Groceries, 98.7% to 99.3% of rulewise's rules were still productive on held-out baskets, against 48.8% for a classical list. The price is recall. See Comparison and Limitations.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
This page documents the public objects exported from rulewise:

from rulewise import RuleMiner, RuleClassifier, ValidationReport
from rulewise import adjust_pvalues, fisher_greater, wilson_interval

docs.title: RuleMiner
docs.text:
RuleMiner(
    min_support=0.01,
    min_confidence=0.1,
    max_antecedent=3,
    max_consequent=1,
    alpha=0.05,
    correction="holm",
    mode="holdout",
    holdout_fraction=0.5,
    n_bootstrap=200,
    backend="auto",
    max_cache_mb=128.0,
    random_state=0,
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameter type default meaning min_support float 0.01 minimum fraction of exploration transactions containing an itemset min_confidence float 0.1 candidate rules below this confidence are not tested max_antecedent int 3 maximum number of items on the left side max_consequent int 1 maximum number of items on the right side alpha float 0.05 significance level after correction, in (0, 1] correction str "holm" "holm", "bonferroni", "bh", "by" or "none" mode str "holdout" "holdout" or "direct" holdout_fraction float 0.5 share of transactions reserved for testing in holdout mode n_bootstrap int 200 resamples for lift and leverage intervals; 0 disables them backend str "auto" "auto", "python" or "pyfim" max_cache_mb float 128.0 memory bound for cached itemset intersections during testing random_state int 0 seed for the split, bootstrap and validation resampling

correction="none" disables multiple-testing correction. It is useful for diagnostics, not for claims of significance.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
attribute type meaning rules_ pandas.DataFrame significant rules, one row per rule diagnostics_ dict mode, backend, counts and replication rate vocab_ dict item name to integer id items_ dict integer id to item name n_features_in_ int number of matrix columns, when fitted on a matrix

diagnostics_ contains:

key meaning mode "holdout" or "direct" backend backend actually used honest_estimates True when holdout mode used a non-empty holdout part n_transactions total transactions n_explore, n_holdout sizes of the exploration and holdout parts n_frequent_itemsets itemsets enumerated n_candidates candidate rules tested n_significant rules returned replication_rate share of tested candidates with unadjusted p below alpha, holdout mode only

docs.title: fit
docs.text:
fit(X, y=None, item_names=None) -> RuleMiner

Fit on transactions: an iterable of item collections, a 0/1 matrix, scipy sparse, pandas or polars. y is ignored and exists for scikit-learn pipeline compatibility. item_names labels matrix columns with strings.

docs.title: transform
docs.text:
transform(transactions) -> numpy.ndarray

Boolean matrix of shape (n_transactions, n_rules). Entry [i, j] is True when rule j's antecedent is contained in transaction i. Returns shape (n, 0) when no rule was found.

docs.title: recommend
docs.text:
recommend(basket, k=5, by="confidence_low", explain=False)

Rank items not in the basket using the significant rules that fire on it. Each item is scored by its best matching rule on by: "confidence_low" (Wilson lower bound, the default), "confidence", "lift" or "leverage". Returns [(item, score)], or a DataFrame with the rule behind each recommendation when explain=True.

confidence_low discounts rules that rest on little data. It is not a probability calibration guarantee; evaluate recommendations on held-out data.

docs.title: stability
docs.text:
stability(transactions, n_resamples=20, fraction=0.8) -> dict

Refit on random subsamples and measure how much the rule set changes. Returns mean_jaccard (mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of the rule sets) and rule_frequency, a DataFrame with the share of subsamples in which each rule from the full fit reappears. Subsamples hold less data than the full fit, so frequencies below 1 are expected even for genuine rules. Compare rules with each other rather than reading a frequency as a probability.

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
validate(transactions, n_null=20, n_stability=0) -> ValidationReport

Refit on n_null datasets with the same item frequencies but no associations. A sound pipeline returns almost nothing; the share of null datasets with at least one rule estimates the empirical family-wise error rate. Also reports holdout replication and, when n_stability > 0, stability. See ValidationReport.

docs.title: query
docs.text:
query(
    min_lift=None,
    min_confidence=None,
    min_support=None,
    max_p=None,
    contains=None,
    antecedent_contains=None,
    consequent_contains=None,
    max_antecedent=None,
    sort_by=None,
    ascending=False,
    top=None,
) -> pandas.DataFrame

Filter and sort the significant rules. contains, antecedent_contains and consequent_contains take one item or a list of items that must all be present. max_p filters on the adjusted p-value. sort_by takes any column name. The result is a new DataFrame.

docs.title: export
docs.text:
export(path, **query_kwargs) -> path

Write the filtered rules to .csv, .json or .parquet and return the path. Tuple columns are flattened to readable strings such as "milk & bread" and "not eggs". Parquet needs pyarrow.

docs.title: to_polars
docs.text:
to_polars(**query_kwargs) -> polars.DataFrame

Same as export, but returns a polars DataFrame. Requires polars.

docs.title: summary
docs.text:
summary(top=5) -> str

Human-readable summary: number of significant rules, candidates tested, and the top rules by adjusted p-value.

docs.title: plot
docs.text:
plot(kind="effect", **kwargs)

kind is "effect" (lift against significance), "forest" (intervals) or "network". Requires matplotlib. Returns the matplotlib axes.

docs.title: RuleClassifier
docs.text:
RuleClassifier(
    min_support=0.01,
    min_confidence=0.0,
    max_antecedent=3,
    alpha=0.05,
    correction="holm",
    mode="direct",
    holdout_fraction=0.5,
    backend="auto",
    max_cache_mb=128.0,
    add_negations=False,
    class_conditional=True,
    random_state=0,
)

RuleClassifier mines rules antecedent -> class, keeps only significant and productive ones, and predicts with the best matching rule ordered by the Wilson lower bound on confidence. When no rule matches, it returns the class priors.

docs.title: Additional parameters
docs.text:
parameter type default meaning add_negations bool False add a ("not", item) item for every feature a row lacks class_conditional bool True mine each class separately for speed; yields the same rules as the general miner

min_support is a fraction of all training transactions, so rules for rare classes need a lower value than rules for common ones.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: attribute type meaning rules_ pandas.DataFrame significant class-association rules classes_ numpy.ndarray class labels in sorted order priors_ numpy.ndarray training class frequencies miner_ RuleMiner the fitted internal miner diagnostics_ dict same keys as RuleMiner.diagnostics_ n_features_in_ int number of matrix columns, when fitted on a matrix

docs.title: fit
docs.text:
fit(X, y, item_names=None) -> RuleClassifier

X accepts the same formats as RuleMiner.fit. y must have one label per row.

docs.title: predict
docs.text:
predict(X) -> numpy.ndarray

Class label for each row.

docs.title: predict_proba
docs.text:
predict_proba(X) -> numpy.ndarray

Class probabilities. When a rule fires for class c with confidence conf, P(c) is conf and the remaining probability is shared among the other classes in proportion to their training priors. For two classes this is exactly the rule's estimated probability for each class. When no rule fires, the class priors are returned.

docs.title: score
docs.text:
score(X, y) -> float

Mean accuracy, as in scikit-learn.

docs.title: explain
docs.text:
explain(X) -> list[dict | None]

For each row, a dict describing the rule that determined its probabilities, or None when no rule matched.

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
validate(X, y, n_null=20, cv=5) -> ValidationReport

Permute the labels n_null times and refit. A sound pipeline finds almost no rules when the labels are random. Also runs cv-fold cross-validation and compares accuracy and log-loss with the majority-class and class-prior baselines.

docs.title: query, export, to_polars, summary, plot
docs.text: The same helpers as RuleMiner. On a classifier, query adds a consequent column rendered as class=<label> so filters and exports work the same way.

docs.title: RuleMiner.rules_
docs.text:
column meaning antecedent tuple of item names consequent tuple of item names support support in the measurement data confidence confidence in the measurement data lift confidence divided by the consequent base rate leverage support minus the independence expectation conviction (1 - P(Y)) / (1 - confidence), or infinity at confidence 1 count transactions containing antecedent and consequent count_antecedent transactions containing the antecedent count_consequent transactions containing the consequent p_value exact productivity p-value p_adjusted p-value after correction confidence_low, confidence_high Wilson interval lift_low, lift_high bootstrap interval, when n_bootstrap > 0 leverage_low, leverage_high bootstrap interval, when n_bootstrap > 0

In holdout mode the counts and measures come from the holdout part. In direct mode they come from the full data and are in-sample estimates.

When a fit returns no significant rules, rules_ keeps the core columns but omits the interval columns. transform returns an array of shape (n, 0) in that case.

docs.title: RuleClassifier.rules_
docs.text: Same measures as RuleMiner.rules_, with class_ instead of consequent and without conviction. confidence_low, confidence_high, lift, leverage, count_antecedent and count_consequent are always present. Use query or explain to see the class label.

docs.title: ValidationReport
docs.text: ValidationReport is a dict with a readable summary() and __str__. Keys depend on the estimator and options.

docs.title: RuleMiner.validate
docs.text: key meaning mode, alpha settings used honest_estimates True when holdout mode used a non-empty holdout part n_rules_real rules found on the real data replication_rate share of candidates with unadjusted p below alpha, holdout mode null_runs number of null datasets null_rule_counts rules found in each null dataset null_mean_rules mean rules per null dataset null_fwer share of null datasets with at least one rule null_fwer_ci Wilson interval on that share calibrated True when the lower confidence bound is at or below alpha null_kind description of the null model stability_resamples number of stability subsamples, when requested stability_mean_jaccard mean pairwise Jaccard overlap, when requested rule_frequency DataFrame of per-rule reappearance rates, when requested

docs.title: RuleClassifier.validate
docs.text: Adds cv_folds, cv_accuracy, cv_accuracy_sd, majority_accuracy, cv_log_loss and prior_log_loss to the null-calibration keys.

docs.title: Statistical helpers
docs.text:
fisher_greater(a, b, c, d) -> float

One-sided Fisher exact p-value for the table [[a, b], [c, d]], testing whether the first row is enriched in the first column. Degenerate margins return 1.0.

adjust_pvalues(pvalues, method="holm") -> numpy.ndarray

Multiple-testing adjustment. Methods: "none", "bonferroni", "holm", "bh", "by". bonferroni and holm control the family-wise error rate. bh and by control the false discovery rate; by holds under arbitrary dependence.

wilson_interval(k, n, alpha=0.05) -> tuple[float, float]

Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion.

docs.title: Input formats
docs.text:
input accepted notes list or generator of lists, sets or tuples yes items must be hashable 2D numpy array yes any numeric dtype; nonzero means present scipy sparse matrix yes any sparse format pandas DataFrame yes dense or sparse one-hot pandas Series of lists yes each element is an item collection polars DataFrame yes one-hot, or a single list column polars Series of lists yes each element is an item collection a bare string no split or encode it first

Matrix input sets n_features_in_ and checks the column count at transform and predict time. NaN, infinity, complex numbers and zero-width matrices are rejected with a ValueError.

docs.title: Scikit-learn integration
docs.text:
RuleMiner is a transformer and RuleClassifier is a classifier. They work in pipelines, GridSearchCV, cross_val_score and RepeatedStratifiedKFold. Numeric features must be discretized first, for example with KBinsDiscretizer(encode="onehot").

The estimator tags declare sparse input support. NotFittedError is raised when a method that needs a fitted model is called before fit.

docs.title: Comparison with existing libraries
docs.text:
This page summarises the head-to-head evaluation in benchmarks/COMPARISON.md. The full report is generated by benchmarks/library_comparison.py and can be reproduced with the commands at the end of this page.

Tested on 2026-11-12 with Python 3.12.4, mlxtend 0.25.0, numpy 2.3.5, pandas 3.1.1 and scipy 1.18.1.

docs.title: Correctness
docs.text:
Frequent itemsets and absolute counts are identical to mlxtend's fpgrowth on Groceries at minimum support 0.02, 0.01, 0.005 and 0.002:

minimum support mlxtend itemsets rulewise itemsets identical 0.02 122 122 yes 0.01 333 333 yes 0.005 1,001 1,001 yes 0.002 4,223 4,223 yes

The statistical layer is an addition, not a different miner.

docs.title: Pure noise
docs.text:
500 independent null datasets, 3,000 transactions, 25 items, varied item frequencies. Nominal level 0.05.

method mean rules datasets with at least one rule rate (95% CI) mlxtend 1,929 500/500 1.000 rulewise holdout 0.02 4/500 0.008 (0.003-0.020) rulewise direct 0.01 4/500 0.008 (0.003-0.020)

The four false-positive datasets each returned one association as two symmetric rules. That is a legitimate 5% level false discovery, not a bug. mlxtend's rules were also tested on a fresh null sample: 4.2% replicated, about what chance predicts.

docs.title: Groceries
docs.text:
Five random halves. Rules were found on one half and evaluated on the other. "Productive" means the rule still beats every simpler version of itself on the held-out half.

method rules productive on held-out lift > 1 productive rules vs classical fit classical all 670 48.8% 98.5% 100% 0.19 s classical lift >= 2 350 48.9% 99.9% 52.1% - classical top-K by lift 174 47.0% 100% 25.1% - mlxtend plus Fisher and Holm 185 64.9% 100% 37.0% - rulewise holdout 116 98.7% 100% 35.3% 0.05 s rulewise direct 174 99.3% 100% 53.6% 0.07 s

Classical rules on this data are mostly real: 98.5% still have lift above 1 on held-out baskets. Their problem is redundancy, not statistical falsehood. About half are no longer productive once simpler rules are considered. rulewise keeps 98% to 99% of what it returns productive, at the cost of recall.

The mlxtend plus Fisher and Holm row is the strongest classical statistical baseline: select candidates on one half, test the 2x2 association on the other half, correct with Holm. Only 3.1% of those rules survived the productivity test on a third evaluation in the planted benchmark. A significant association is not the same as a non-redundant rule.

docs.title: Planted rules
docs.text:
Five datasets, 20,000 baskets, 30 items, four planted rules and 15% noise. Rules were mined on one half and evaluated on the other.

method rules productive on test planted recall exact planted precision reliable F1 classical all 15,685 1.4% 100% 0.0% 0.03 classical top-35 by lift 35 9.1% 65% 7.4% 0.16 classical top-35 by confidence 35 1.1% 0% 0.0% 0.00 mlxtend plus Fisher and Holm 3,486 3.1% 100% 0.1% 0.06 rulewise holdout 35 100.0% 100% 11.4% 1.00 rulewise direct 35 100.0% 100% 11.4% 1.00

The exact planted precision is low because rulewise also returns genuine sub-rules and reverse rules, not because it returns false rules. The reliable F1 combines productive precision with planted recall; read it as a summary of a trustworthy set, not as a count of planted rules.

docs.title: Fit time
docs.text:
Single core, this machine. rulewise was faster than mlxtend in these runs even though it tests every candidate, because it never materialises the full rule list.

data mlxtend efficient-apriori rulewise holdout rulewise direct Groceries, 169 items, support 0.005 0.35 s 0.17 s 0.08 s 0.09 s synthetic, 20k x 30, support 0.01 2.62 s 8.25 s 0.62 s 0.75 s dense null, 50k x 60, support 0.0005 8.39 s 119.33 s 2.75 s 4.26 s

Speed is not the contribution. The statistical pass grows with the number of candidates, so dense data at low support can be slow. The optional PyFIM backend was not testable on Python 3.12 and Windows; the core uses the pure-Python backend.

docs.title: Classifier
docs.text:
UCI Mushrooms, 5-fold cross-validation with 3 repeats. Accuracy and log-loss.

model accuracy log-loss rules majority class 0.518 0.693 - logistic regression 0.9998 0.0007 - decision tree, depth 6 0.9959 0.0141 - rulewise holdout 0.9957 0.0209 1,042 rulewise direct 0.9970 0.0113 1,373

Mushrooms is a best case for an associative classifier: categorical features and strong conjunctions. rulewise is competitive but does not beat logistic regression. On dense numeric data the gap is much larger; see Limitations.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
One hidden item per held-out Groceries basket, hit@5:

method hit@5 coverage popularity 26.4% 100% classical all 20.1% 92.7% rulewise holdout 18.7% 85.3% rulewise direct 19.7% 90.2%

A popularity baseline wins on raw hit rate. Use recommend when you need an explanation, not when you need the best hit rate.

docs.title: What the comparison supports
docs.text:
Supported:

  • exact frequent-itemset mining;
  • empirical error control on null data;
  • much higher held-out productivity than a classical list;
  • honest effect sizes in holdout mode;
  • a compact, readable rule set;
  • speed at these scales;
  • a scikit-learn-compatible API.

Not supported:

  • higher recall than a classical list;
  • better recommendation hit rate than popularity;
  • better classification than logistic regression or a tree;
  • a full replacement for mlxtend's feature set (closed itemsets, many metrics, constraints).

docs.title: Positioning
docs.text: Use mlxtend when you want the full classical catalogue, many metrics, or closed and maximal itemsets. Use rulewise when a short, statistically vetted list matters more than recall, and when you need to defend each rule to a reviewer, an auditor or a domain expert.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python benchmarks/get_data.py
python benchmarks/library_comparison.py --section all --runs 500 --seeds 5 \
       --out benchmarks/COMPARISON.md

The internal review with the full discussion is in benchmarks/PRE_PUBLISH_REVIEW.md.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: No method is free of trade-offs. These are the limits that matter when deciding whether rulewise is appropriate, with the measured evidence where it exists.

docs.title: Recall is lower than a classical list
docs.text:
The error guarantee is conservative. On Groceries, rulewise returned about half as many held-out-productive rules as a classical list in direct mode, and about a third in holdout mode. If your goal is to collect every possible candidate and filter by hand, a classical miner is a larger haystack.

The power study in benchmarks/RESULTS.md shows the same effect. With 20 planted 3-item patterns among 1,000 items, n = 5,000 and minimum support 0.001, rulewise recovered 9 of 20 patterns in holdout mode and 11 of 20 in direct mode at the weakest signal. It recovered 20 of 20 once the signal was stronger (strength 0.005 and above), with zero false rules. Weak effects need more data.

Mitigations:

  • use direct mode if you need power and can accept optimistic effect sizes;
  • lower min_support and min_confidence, at the cost of more candidates and a slower fit;
  • increase the sample size;
  • use alpha=0.1 if a 10% family-wise error rate is acceptable for exploration, and confirm on a fresh sample.

docs.title: Redundancy is reduced, not eliminated
docs.text:
The productivity test removes rules whose extra antecedent items add nothing. It does not remove nested sub-rules or reverse rules. In the planted benchmark, four planted structures produced 35 returned rules: the four planted rules, their sub-rules, and their reverse directions. All 35 were productive on held-out data, so they are not false positives, but the set is not minimal.

If you need a smaller set, use query to filter by antecedent size or confidence, or add a non-redundant or self-sufficient-itemset post-processing step. A built-in minimal-rule mode is a natural next feature, not something the current release guarantees.

docs.title: Basket size and other confounders
docs.text:
The test asks whether two items are independent. Items that co-occur only because some baskets are larger are dependent, so a rule can be reported even though the extra item does not cause the other. The same applies to a third variable that drives both items. The shuffle null in validate preserves item frequencies but does not model basket-size effects or confounding.

This is a property of the null hypothesis, not a bug: the rule is a real association in the sample. It is not evidence of causation or of a useful intervention.

docs.title: Independent and identically distributed rows
docs.text:
All p-values assume exchangeable transactions. Repeated baskets from the same household, grouped or clustered data, time series, and survey weights violate this. The effective sample size is smaller than the row count, and the p-values can be too small.

Mitigations:

  • split by group, not by row, when fitting and validating;
  • use a holdout part that is independent in the same sense;
  • treat the output as descriptive, not confirmatory, when the rows are not exchangeable.

docs.title: Direct mode effect sizes are optimistic
docs.text:
In direct mode, the same data selects the rules and estimates their confidence and lift. Rules are selected partly because their effect is large in that sample, so the reported effects are biased upward. This is the winner's curse. The p-values remain valid under the layered correction, but the confidence and lift columns do not.

Use holdout mode when you need honest effect sizes, or validate direct-mode rules on a fresh sample.

docs.title: Small samples and rare items
docs.text:
A rule with a small count can have a large lift and a wide interval. The Wilson interval and the bootstrap interval show this, but the point estimate can still mislead. Items that occur in every transaction are excluded because they cannot appear in a significant rule. Rare items may never reach the support floor.

Raise min_support for dense data to keep the candidate count manageable. Lower it only when the sample is large enough for the resulting counts to be meaningful.

docs.title: Dense numeric data
docs.text:
rulewise predicts or describes with conjunctions of discrete items. Numeric features must be binned first. Signal spread thinly across many numeric features is a weak case: each rule covers a small region, and prediction uses one best rule rather than accumulating evidence. On digits, the classifier reached about 0.61 accuracy against 0.97 for logistic regression. Use a linear model or a tree ensemble when accuracy is the goal.

Binning also matters. Quantile bins inside each training fold avoid leakage. Too many bins produce sparse items; too few lose signal.

docs.title: Positive associations only
docs.text: Candidate rules require lift above 1. rulewise does not report negative associations, rules with lift below 1, or independence rules. It also does not mine closed or maximal itemsets, does not support item constraints, and does not implement top-k mining. mlxtend and other libraries cover some of those cases.

docs.title: Recommendation quality
docs.text: recommend is an explainable interface, not a state-of-the-art recommender. On Groceries with one hidden item per basket, hit@5 was 18.7% in holdout mode and 19.7% in direct mode. A popularity baseline reached 26.4%, and a classical rule list reached 20.1%. The value of recommend is that every recommendation names the rule behind it, not that it maximizes hit rate.

docs.title: Classification is competitive, not superior
docs.text: On categorical data with a few strong conjunctions, such as Mushrooms, the classifier is close to logistic regression: 0.9970 accuracy against 0.9998. On Titanic it is a few points behind logistic regression and a depth-4 tree. The advantage is readability and an interval on every rule, not accuracy.

docs.title: Multiple testing is conservative
docs.text:
The empirical family-wise error rate on null data is about 0.8% at a nominal 5%, not 5%. The correction and the productivity test are both conservative, and discreteness of the Fisher test adds further conservatism. This is deliberate: the method is designed to avoid false rules rather than to maximize discoveries.

The practical consequence is that a null result does not prove independence. It means the data did not provide enough evidence at the chosen error rate. Report the candidate count, the sample size and the support floor alongside the result.

docs.title: PyFIM is optional and legacy
docs.text: PyFIM is a C extension with wheels only for old Python versions. It is not installed by default and the core package uses the pure-Python backend. The pure-Python backend produced identical itemsets in the tests and was faster than mlxtend on the benchmark datasets, so PyFIM is not needed for typical use.

docs.title: No causal claims
docs.text: A significant rule is an association in the sample. It is not evidence that changing the antecedent will change the consequent. Confounding, selection and reverse causation remain possible. Use domain knowledge and, when possible, an experiment before acting on a rule.

docs.title: What to report
docs.text:
When publishing results, report:

  • the mode and alpha;
  • the correction method;
  • min_support, min_confidence, max_antecedent and max_consequent;
  • the number of transactions and the number of candidates tested;
  • the null calibration result from validate, with the number of null runs;
  • the recall limitation, especially if the rule set is used as a complete catalogue.

These are the numbers a reader needs to judge whether the guarantee applies to the analysis.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: This page explains what rulewise computes and why the result can be called statistically sound. The implementation follows the productive-rule framework of Webb (2007, 2008, 2010) and the tutorial of Hamalainen and Webb (2019).

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
A rule X -> Y is a claim that transactions containing X are more likely to contain Y than transactions that do not contain X. A classical miner applies minimum support and minimum confidence and returns every rule that passes. That procedure tests an enormous number of hypotheses without accounting for the number tested, so the chance of returning at least one spurious rule rises with the search space. On pure noise, a classical miner still returns thousands of rules.

rulewise treats rule discovery as multiple hypothesis testing. It tests each candidate, corrects for the number of tests, and reports the corrected p-value.

docs.title: The 2x2 table
docs.text:
For a rule X -> Y, count the four cells over the measurement data:

Y present Y absent X present a b X absent c d

a is the number of transactions containing both sides, a + b the number containing X, a + c the number containing Y, and n = a + b + c + d the total.

Support, confidence, lift, leverage and conviction are computed from these counts:

support    = a / n
confidence = a / (a + b)
lift       = confidence / ((a + c) / n)
leverage   = support - ((a + b) / n) * ((a + c) / n)
conviction = (1 - (a + c) / n) / (1 - confidence)

docs.title: The productivity test
docs.text:
A frequent and confident rule can still be redundant. If A already predicts Y, then A and B -> Y may add nothing: the extra item B may simply ride along. Webb calls a rule productive if its confidence is higher than the confidence of every proper subset of its antecedent:

productive(X -> Y) = for every proper subset Z of X:
                         confidence(X -> Y) > confidence(Z -> Y)

rulewise tests each comparison with a one-sided Fisher exact test on the measurement data. For a subset Z, the test asks whether adding X - Z raises the rate of Y among transactions that already contain Z.

The rule's p-value is the maximum over all comparisons. This is an intersection-union test: the rule is declared significant only if every comparison is significant. It controls the type I error for the null "this rule is not productive" without an additional correction across the comparisons, because the maximum of the p-values is itself a valid p-value for the intersection of the null hypotheses.

For a rule with more than one item in the consequent, rulewise also requires significant positive dependence across every bipartition of the full itemset. An item that is merely carried along by the others makes the rule fail. This is the self-sufficient-itemset idea of Webb (2010). The reported p-value is the maximum of the productivity p-value and the partition p-value.

Immediate subsets are tested first. When a comparison already reaches the cap, the search stops and returns a value at or above the cap. Any p-value below the cap is exact; a value above the cap is a lower bound, which is enough to decide that the rule is not significant.

docs.title: Multiple testing
docs.text: The candidates are not independent, and the number of possible rules is large. rulewise offers two families of corrections.

docs.title: Family-wise error rate
docs.text: correction="holm" (default) or "bonferroni" controls the probability of returning at least one spurious rule at or below alpha. Holm is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni and is the recommended default.

docs.title: False discovery rate
docs.text:
correction="bh" (Benjamini-Hochberg) or "by" (Benjamini-Yekutieli) controls the expected share of false discoveries among the returned rules. by is valid under arbitrary dependence and is more conservative than bh.

Use FDR when you can tolerate a small share of false rules in exchange for more true ones. Use FWER when a single false rule is unacceptable.

correction="none" disables adjustment. It is for diagnostics only.

docs.title: Holdout mode
docs.text:
In holdout mode, rulewise splits the transactions into an exploration part and a holdout part. Candidates are generated on the exploration part, using minimum support and confidence. Each candidate is then tested with the productivity test on the holdout part, and all reported measures and intervals are computed there. Because the holdout part was not used to choose the candidates, the tests and effect sizes are honest.

The cost is statistical power: the miner sees only part of the data, and rules that are frequent in the full data may not reach the support floor in the exploration part.

holdout_fraction controls the split. The default is 0.5. A value of 0 disables the split and raises a warning because the p-values are then not valid.

docs.title: Direct mode
docs.text:
In direct mode, all data are used for both candidate generation and testing. To keep the family-wise error rate valid when the hypotheses are selected from the same data, rulewise uses Webb's layered critical values:

  • rules are grouped by total size l = |X| + |Y|;
  • alpha is divided equally across the layers;
  • within a layer, a Bonferroni correction is applied over the number of rules that could possibly be reported at that size, not only the candidates that passed the filters.

For a rule at level l, the critical value is:

alpha / (number_of_layers * search_space_size[l])

This is why direct mode remains valid even though the support and confidence filters are applied to the same data. It is conservative when there are many items, because the search space grows combinatorially. On small data it is often more powerful than holdout mode because it uses every transaction.

The reported confidence, lift and intervals in direct mode are measured on the same data that selected the rules. They are optimistically biased by the winner's curse. Use holdout mode when effect sizes matter; use direct mode when detection matters more.

docs.title: Intervals
docs.text:
Confidence intervals use the Wilson score interval, which behaves better than the normal approximation for small counts and proportions near 0 or 1.

Lift and leverage intervals use a percentile bootstrap. Resampling transactions with replacement is equivalent to drawing the four cell counts from a multinomial distribution with the observed cell proportions, so no transaction-level resampling is needed. The interval reflects the uncertainty in the 2x2 table, not model uncertainty.

docs.title: Candidate generation
docs.text:
Frequent itemsets are mined with a bitset Eclat implementation. For every frequent itemset S and every split S = X union Y with 1 <= |Y| <= max_consequent and |X| <= max_antecedent, a rule is a candidate when its confidence is at least min_confidence and its lift is above 1. Rules with an empty antecedent or consequent are not generated.

The implementation excludes items that occur in every transaction. They cannot appear in a significant rule: as a consequent they have lift 1, and as an antecedent item they add no coverage. This also keeps the Python and PyFIM backends identical.

Class-conditional mining, used by RuleClassifier by default, mines each class separately. It produces the same candidates as the general miner and is much faster on dense data. Items that occur in every row of one class are re-added after mining because they are strong predictors.

docs.title: Assumptions and what they mean
docs.text:
The error guarantee is conditional on these assumptions:

  1. Independent and identically distributed transactions. Repeated baskets, clustering, time dependence or survey weights violate this.
  2. Independence null. The test asks whether X and Y are independent. It does not adjust for basket size, a third variable, or selection of the data.
  3. Independent holdout. In holdout mode, the holdout part must not be used to choose candidates. The default split satisfies this, but do not tune thresholds on the holdout part and then report the same p-values.
  4. Full search space in direct mode. The layered correction counts every rule that could be reported at a size, not only the candidates that passed the filters.
  5. Correct model of the data. The Fisher test assumes the 2x2 table is a random sample from the population of interest. If rows are not exchangeable, the p-value is not meaningful.

Under these assumptions, the probability of one or more false rules is at most alpha with Holm or Bonferroni, and the expected false discovery proportion is at most alpha with BH or BY.

The procedure is conservative. Empirical error rates on null data are well below 5%, which means the method pays for its guarantee with power. This is visible in the low recall on real data and in the power study.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Webb, G.I. (2007). Discovering significant patterns. Machine Learning 68(1), 1-33.
  • Webb, G.I. (2008). Layered critical values: a powerful direct-adjustment approach to discovering significant patterns. Machine Learning 71(2-3), 307-323.
  • Webb, G.I. (2010). Self-sufficient itemsets: an approach to screening potentially interesting associations. ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data 4(1), 1-20.
  • Hamalainen, W. and Webb, G.I. (2019). A tutorial on statistically sound pattern discovery. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 33, 325-377.
  • Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 6, 65-70.
  • Benjamini, Y. and Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 57, 289-300.
  • Benjamini, Y. and Yekutieli, D. (2001). The control of the false discovery rate in multiple testing under dependency. Annals of Statistics 29, 1165-1188.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text: This page is the release checklist. The package name rulewise is available on PyPI as of 2026-11-12. The version is set in pyproject.toml and src/rulewise/__init__.py; keep the two in sync.

docs.title: 1. Preflight
docs.text:
python -m pytest -q
python -m build --sdist --wheel
python -m twine check dist/*

twine check validates the long description and the metadata. If it reports unknown fields such as license-expression or license-file, upgrade packaging to 24.2 or newer, or upgrade twine.

Check the version and the name one more time:

python -c "import rulewise; print(rulewise.__version__)"

A version that already exists on PyPI or TestPyPI cannot be replaced. Bump it before uploading.

docs.title: 2. Build
docs.text:
From a clean tree:

rm -rf build dist src/*.egg-info
python -m build --sdist --wheel
python -m twine check dist/*

The wheel should contain only rulewise and its metadata. The source distribution also contains the tests, the benchmarks, the docs and the changelog. Public datasets are not bundled; users run python benchmarks/get_data.py if they want to reproduce the benchmarks.

docs.title: 3. Upload to TestPyPI first
docs.text:
Create a TestPyPI account and an API token, then:

python -m twine upload --repository testpypi dist/*

Install from TestPyPI in a clean environment:

python -m pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ \
    --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ rulewise
python -c "import rulewise; print(rulewise.__version__)"

Use the extra index so that numpy, scipy and pandas come from PyPI.

docs.title: 4. Upload to PyPI
docs.text:
Create a PyPI API token scoped to the rulewise project. Use __token__ as the username:

python -m twine upload dist/*

Twine reads TWINE_USERNAME and TWINE_PASSWORD from the environment, or from ~/.pypirc, or from the keyring. Never commit a token and never pass it on a command line that is recorded in shell history. A typical local flow is:

export TWINE_USERNAME=__token__
export TWINE_PASSWORD=pypi-...
python -m twine upload dist/*

On Windows PowerShell:

$env:TWINE_USERNAME = "__token__"
$env:TWINE_PASSWORD = "pypi-..."
python -m twine upload dist/*

docs.title: 5. Preferred: trusted publishing from GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The repository includes .github/workflows/publish.yml. It builds the distributions, checks them, and publishes with OIDC trusted publishing when a GitHub release is published. No PyPI token is stored in the repository.

One-time setup on PyPI:

  1. Open the project on PyPI, then Publishing, then Add a trusted publisher.
  2. Choose GitHub.
  3. Enter owner ShadowGodd1, repository Rulewise, workflow filename publish.yml, and environment name pypi.
  4. Save.

Then create a GitHub release with a tag such as v0.1.0. The workflow publishes the version in pyproject.toml; the tag is only a label.

If you prefer a token-based workflow, add PYPI_API_TOKEN as a repository secret and pass it to pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish with password: ${{ secrets.PYPI_API_TOKEN }}.

docs.title: 6. After upload
docs.text:
• Check the PyPI page: README rendering, classifiers, project links, licence and Python requirement.
  • Install the released wheel in a clean environment and run the five-minute example.
  • Tag the release in version control.
  • Update CHANGELOG.md with the release date and move unreleased items under the version.
  • Build and deploy the documentation site if you maintain one.

docs.title: Documentation site
docs.text:
The docs are plain Markdown with a mkdocs.yml configuration. The docs workflow builds and pushes them to the gh-pages branch. Enable GitHub Pages once in the repository settings:

  1. Open Settings, then Pages.
  2. Under Build and deployment, choose Deploy from a branch.
  3. Select the gh-pages branch and the root folder.

The site is then served at https://shadowgodd1.github.io/Rulewise/. To build locally:

pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material
python -m mkdocs build --strict
python -m mkdocs serve

python -m mkdocs build --strict fails on broken internal links and missing pages. Run it before a release if the documentation site is part of the announcement. Newer versions of mkdocs-material print an end-of-life notice that strict mode treats as a warning; set NO_MKDOCS_2_WARNING=1 in CI if you see that message.

docs.title: invalid-publisher: no corresponding publisher
docs.text:
This means the OIDC token is valid but PyPI has no pending or normal trusted publisher that matches the claims. For this repository the values must be exact:

field on PyPI value PyPI project name rulewise Owner ShadowGodd1 Repository name Rulewise Workflow name publish.yml Environment name pypi

Add it at https://pypi.org/manage/account/publishing/ before the first upload. For a new project this is a pending publisher, not a publisher on an existing project. After saving, re-run the failed publish workflow or push a new tag.

The claims printed in the error should include:

repository: ShadowGodd1/Rulewise
workflow_ref: ShadowGodd1/Rulewise/.github/workflows/publish.yml@refs/tags/v0.1.0
environment: pypi

If any of those differ, fix the workflow or the publisher configuration. Do not copy the sub claim into the form; the form fields are the five values in the table above.

docs.title: Token upload instead of OIDC
docs.text:
A project-scoped PyPI API token also works. Create one at https://pypi.org/manage/account/token/ and either upload locally with twine or add it as a repository secret and pass it to the action:

- uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1
  with:
    password: ${{ secrets.PYPI_API_TOKEN }}

Remove the id-token: write permission only if you stop using trusted publishing.

docs.title: Version policy
docs.text: Use semantic versioning. Before 1.0, minor releases may change behaviour. A release that changes the default mode, the correction, the output columns or the meaning of an existing parameter is a breaking change and needs a minor version bump with a migration note in CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Tests pass: python -m pytest -q
  • [ ] Version is correct in pyproject.toml and src/rulewise/__init__.py
  • [ ] CHANGELOG.md has an entry for the version
  • [ ] python -m build succeeds
  • [ ] python -m twine check dist/* passes
  • [ ] TestPyPI install works
  • [ ] PyPI upload uses a scoped token or trusted publishing
  • [ ] Clean install from PyPI runs the five-minute example
  • [ ] Documentation builds with mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Tutorial: classification with rules (Mushrooms and Titanic)
docs.text:
Two real categorical datasets, downloaded rather than bundled. In a checkout of the repository, run python benchmarks/get_data.py; otherwise download them directly:

curl -L -o mushrooms.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stedy/Machine-Learning-with-R-datasets/master/mushrooms.csv
curl -L -o titanic.csv   https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mwaskom/seaborn-data/master/titanic.csv

docs.title: Mushrooms: 8,124 mushrooms, 22 categorical features, edible or poisonous
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from rulewise import RuleClassifier

d = pd.read_csv("mushrooms.csv")
y = (d["type"] == "p").to_numpy()                       # poisonous
X = pd.get_dummies(d.drop(columns="type"), prefix_sep="=").astype(bool)

clf = RuleClassifier(min_support=0.01, max_antecedent=3)
clf.fit(X.to_numpy(), y, item_names=list(X.columns))
clf.rules_[["antecedent", "class_", "confidence", "confidence_low", "support"]]
clf.explain(X.to_numpy()[:1])                           # the rule behind a prediction

Strong rules it finds (fit on all data; the interval is the 95% Wilson interval). This is a selection, not the full list:

gill_size=b & odor=n & ring_number=o         -> poisonous=False  conf=1.000 [0.999,1.000] support=0.331
odor=n & stalk_shape=t                       -> poisonous=False  conf=1.000 [0.998,1.000] support=0.307
gill_spacing=c & stalk_surface_above_ring=k  -> poisonous=True   conf=1.000 [0.998,1.000] support=0.274
odor=f                                       -> poisonous=True   conf=1.000 [0.998,1.000] support=0.266

odor=f (a foul smell) being a perfect poison indicator is the classic finding for this dataset.

Cross-validated (5-fold x 3 repeats; benchmarks/real_classification.py):

model accuracy log-loss rules majority class 0.518 0.693 logistic regression 1.000 0.006 decision tree (depth 4) 0.991 0.043 RuleClassifier (direct) 0.997 0.011 1,373 RuleClassifier (holdout) 0.996 0.021 1,042

Rules come close to logistic regression but do not beat it, and 1,373 rules is a lot to read: many are different routes to the same conclusion because this dataset has many redundant, correlated attributes. Use query (for example min_confidence, max_antecedent=1) to look at the short, strong ones first.

docs.title: Titanic: 891 passengers, survived or not
docs.text:
Features are one-hot: class, sex, age band, having siblings/spouse, having parents/children, port, fare tercile.

fare=high & no_parent_or_child & sex=female  -> survived=True   conf=0.984 [0.917,0.997] support=0.071
class=1 & sex=female                         -> survived=True   conf=0.968 [0.910,0.989] support=0.102
fare=low & sex=male                          -> survived=False  conf=0.894 [0.850,0.926] support=0.255
class=2 & sex=female                         -> survived=True   conf=0.921 [0.838,0.963] support=0.079
sex=male                                     -> survived=False  conf=0.811 [0.777,0.841] support=0.525
class=3 & port=S                             -> survived=False  conf=0.810 [0.766,0.848] support=0.321
model accuracy log-loss rules majority class 0.616 0.666 logistic regression 0.790 0.464 decision tree (depth 4) 0.818 0.493 RuleClassifier (direct) 0.777 0.529 14 RuleClassifier (holdout) 0.773 0.543 7

Here the rules are a few points behind logistic regression and the tree. What you get in exchange is a model you can read in a minute, with an interval on every rule.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Use rules where you need an explanation or a short list of statistically defensible patterns on categorical or behavioural data. If you only want maximum accuracy, logistic regression or a tree-based model is as good or better on all of these datasets.

docs.title: Reproducing the numbers
docs.text: The tables are from benchmarks/real_classification.py on the local data files. Download them once with python benchmarks/get_data.py. Exact values can move by a few thousandths across library versions; the conclusions do not.

docs.title: Where to next
docs.text:
• API reference for RuleClassifier, predict_proba, explain and validate.
  • Methodology for class-conditional mining and direct mode.
  • Limitations for the numeric-data and accuracy gap.

docs.title: Tutorial: rules from real supermarket baskets (Groceries)
docs.text:
The Groceries dataset has 9,835 real baskets over 169 items (mean basket size 4.4), from the arules R package. It is not bundled with rulewise; download it once:

curl -L -o groceries.csv \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stedy/Machine-Learning-with-R-datasets/master/groceries.csv

All output below was produced by running this code (benchmarks/ has the scripts).

docs.title: Fit
docs.text:
import csv
from rulewise import RuleMiner

tx = [sorted({x.strip() for x in row if x.strip()}) for row in csv.reader(open("groceries.csv"))]
tx = [t for t in tx if t]

miner = RuleMiner(min_support=0.005, max_antecedent=3, random_state=0).fit(tx)
print(miner.summary(top=6))

RuleMiner: 250 significant rules (alpha=0.05, mode=holdout, backend=python); 1563 candidates tested on 4918 transactions
Top 6 by adjusted p-value:
  root vegetables  ->  other vegetables   conf=0.436 [0.395, 0.479]  lift=2.30  p_adj=2.62e-41
  other vegetables  ->  root vegetables   conf=0.249 [0.223, 0.278]  lift=2.30  p_adj=2.62e-41
  root vegetables  ->  beef   conf=0.176 [0.146, 0.211]  lift=3.19  p_adj=2.71e-24
  beef  ->  root vegetables   conf=0.347 [0.293, 0.405]  lift=3.19  p_adj=2.71e-24
  pip fruit  ->  tropical fruit   conf=0.282 [0.239, 0.329]  lift=2.73  p_adj=1.66e-21
  tropical fruit  ->  pip fruit   conf=0.211 [0.177, 0.248]  lift=2.73  p_adj=1.66e-21

Rules were found on one half of the baskets and tested and measured on the other (holdout mode), so the confidences and lifts are honest estimates, with intervals.

docs.title: Strongest associations, with uncertainty
docs.text:
miner.query(min_lift=2.5, sort_by="lift", top=6)

sugar               -> flour          conf=0.13 [0.09,0.19] lift=8.74 [6.12,11.26]
flour               -> sugar          conf=0.29 [0.20,0.40] lift=8.74 [6.09,11.60]
processed cheese    -> white bread    conf=0.22 [0.14,0.32] lift=4.97 [2.86,7.21]
white bread         -> processed cheese conf=0.07 [0.05,0.12] lift=4.97 [3.05,6.81]
whipped/sour cream  -> berries        conf=0.13 [0.10,0.17] lift=3.68 [2.77,4.60]
berries             -> whipped/sour cream conf=0.27 [0.21,0.34] lift=3.68 [2.89,4.49]

Note how wide the lift intervals are for rare items: sugar and flour have a lift of 8.7, but the data only pin it between 6.1 and 11.3. A ranking by lift alone hides that.

docs.title: Recommendations with the rule behind them
docs.text:
miner.recommend(["yogurt", "whole milk"], k=4, explain=True)

               item     score            antecedent
0  other vegetables  0.343362  (whole milk, yogurt)
1        rolls/buns  0.212485             (yogurt,)
2    tropical fruit  0.185759             (yogurt,)
3   root vegetables  0.167799         (whole milk,)

The score is the Wilson lower bound on confidence, so a rule resting on little data is discounted.

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
print(miner.validate(tx, n_null=30, n_stability=10))

rulewise validation report (mode=holdout, alpha=0.05)
  rules found on the real data:        250
  holdout replication (p < alpha):      0.53 of tested candidates
  null calibration (30 shuffled datasets with the same item frequencies):
    datasets producing >= 1 rule:      0/30  -> empirical error rate 0.00 (95% CI 0.00-0.11), consistent with the nominal level
    mean rules per null dataset:       0.00
    note: with only 30 null runs this detects gross miscalibration only
  stability (10 subsamples): mean Jaccard overlap 0.54

How to read it:

  • Null calibration passes: on shuffled copies of this data (same item frequencies, no associations) the pipeline almost never reports anything.
  • Stability 0.54 is a real signal, not a defect: each subsample has only 80% of the data, so borderline rules enter and leave. Use rule_frequency in the report to separate rules that appear in nearly every subsample from borderline ones.

docs.title: Does it beat the classical approach? A held-out test
docs.text:
benchmarks/replication_groceries.py splits the baskets in halves A and B, finds rules on A, and checks them on B (6 random splits). "Classical" is support >= 0.5%, confidence >= 25%, lift > 1, with no statistical testing.

method rules lift > 1 on B still productive on B productive rules on B classical (all) 709 0.91 0.47 331 classical, lift >= 2 376 0.97 0.44 166 classical, top-K by lift 176 0.99 0.43 76 classical, top-K by confidence 176 0.97 0.37 65 rulewise holdout 114 0.99 0.98 112 rulewise direct 176 0.98 0.98 173

(K is set to rulewise's rule count, which gives the classical baselines an advantage.)

What this does and does not show:

  • On this data the classical rules are already mostly real: 91% have lift > 1 on held-out baskets. Raising the lift threshold does not change that much. A supermarket has strong genuine associations, and a 0.5% support floor already removes most noise.
  • The difference is redundancy: only 47% of the classical list is still productive on held-out data (the rest is explained by simpler rules), and no lift or confidence threshold fixes it. 98% of rulewise's rules are productive on baskets they never saw.
  • The price is recall. The classical list contains 331 productive-on-B rules among 378 redundant ones; rulewise direct recovers 173 and holdout 112. If you want every candidate and will filter by hand, the classical list is a bigger haystack.
  • The metric rewards what rulewise optimises (productivity), so read it as validation that the error control generalises, not as a neutral ranking of all uses of rules.

docs.text:

  • Methodology for the statistical test and the two modes.
  • Limitations for power, redundancy and basket-size effects.
  • Comparison for the head-to-head against mlxtend.
